title: Module 23 check: data science and computing

questions.prompt: A model predicting house prices has an RMSE of $12,000 on the 800 houses it was trained on and $31,000 on 200 houses held out. What does this suggest?
options: The model overfits: it fits the training houses' noise and predicts new houses much worse; expect errors near $31,000 in use
The hold-out houses must be wrong
The two errors should be averaged
questions.explanation: A large gap between training and test error is the mark of overfitting. The test error estimates the error on new data; a simpler model (fewer predictors, less flexibility) chosen by cross-validation would likely do better.

questions.prompt: A model predicting whether a customer will cancel uses, among its predictors, "date the account was closed". It scores 99 % on the test set. What is wrong?
options: Data leakage: the predictor is only known after the outcome, so the model cannot be used to predict cancellations in advance
The test set is too large
questions.explanation: A closing date exists only for customers who have already cancelled: it gives the answer away. Every predictor must be known at the time the prediction is made.

questions.prompt: A disease-screening model's confusion matrix: 30 true positives, 20 false negatives, 70 false positives, 880 true negatives. What is its recall? Give it to two decimals.
questions.explanation: Recall = TP/(TP + FN) = 30/(30 + 20) = 0.60: it finds 60 % of the real cases.

questions.prompt: For the same model (TP 30, FN 20, FP 70, TN 880), what is its precision? Give it to two decimals.
questions.explanation: Precision = TP/(TP + FP) = 30/(30 + 70) = 0.30: only 30 % of the cases it flags are real. Its accuracy, (30 + 880)/1000 = 0.91, hides both weaknesses.

questions.prompt: An A/B test of a change that in fact does nothing tracks 10 independent metrics, each tested at α = 0.05. What is the chance that at least one comes out "significant"? Give it to three decimals.
questions.explanation: 1 − 0.95¹⁰ = 1 − 0.599 = 0.401: four tests in ten would "find" a winning metric by chance. Name one primary metric in advance.

questions.prompt: Half of a mailbox is spam (prior odds 1). An email contains two words whose likelihood ratios P(word | spam)/P(word | genuine) are 4 and 5. Assuming the words are independent within each class (naive Bayes), what is the probability the email is spam? Give it to three decimals.
20 % of mail is spam. A word appears in 50 % of spam and 5 % of genuine mail. What is P(spam | word)? Give it to three decimals.

k-means with k = 2 on the values 1, 2, 9, 10, 11, starting from centres 1 and 11. After assigning each value to its nearer centre, what is the new second centre (the mean of the values assigned to 11)? Give it to one decimal.
questions.explanation: 1 and 2 are nearer to 1; 9, 10 and 11 are nearer to 11. The new centres are the means: (1 + 2)/2 = 1.5 and (9 + 10 + 11)/3 = 10.0.

questions.prompt: A sensor's readings have first quartile 20 and third quartile 30. Above what value is a reading flagged as an anomaly by the upper box-plot fence?
questions.explanation: IQR = 30 − 20 = 10; the upper fence is Q₃ + 1.5 IQR = 30 + 15 = 45. The fences use the quartiles, so a few extreme readings do not move them.

questions.prompt: A service runs on two servers in parallel (it works if either works). Each is available 98 % of the time, independently. What is the service's availability? Give it to four decimals.
questions.explanation: It fails only if both fail: (1 − 0.98)² = 0.0004. Availability = 1 − 0.0004 = 0.9996, about 3.5 hours down a year instead of 7.3 days for one server.
